c:borrow_loaned_message.why: RFC-0010's zero-copy path. rcl/rclcpp borrow a TYPED message the middleware owns (`LoanedMessage<T>`, `borrow_loaned_message`, `publish_loaned_message`, `return_loaned_message_from_publisher`); ours is a TOKEN over a byte range (`loan`/`commit`/`discard` on the publisher, `borrow`/`release` on the subscription) because C has no templates and the wrapper would need an allocator to own. NOTE the verbs differ as well as the shape, and only the shape has a reason -- W5 should decide whether `loan`/`commit`/`discard` should read `borrow_loaned_message`/`publish_loaned_message`/`return_loaned_message`.

c:event_publisher_count_cb_t.why: QoS events. rclcpp routes every event through one `set_on_new_qos_event_callback` plus a `QOSEventHandler` waitable the executor polls; ours are named callbacks per event (`on_liveliness_lost`, `on_offered_deadline_missed`, `on_message_lost`) registered on the entity. Constraint: no allocator for a per-event handler object and no wait-set to poll it from -- the callback is a fn-ptr in the entity's own static storage. The set of events is the same. This one reports matched-subscription count changes, which rclcpp answers by POLLING `get_subscription_count` -- see that row.

c:executor_add_subscription_in_group.why: adds a subscription to a named callback group, which rclc has no concept of (rclcpp does -- see `cpp:Node::create_callback_group` in the exec stage). Needed because RFC-0002 maps groups onto RTOS priority tiers.

c:executor_add_subscription_raw.why:
phase-417 stage 6 — the callback moved OFF `*_init` and onto registration, so `rclc_{subscription,service}_init_default` now matches rclc's four-argument shape and the callback arrives here, exactly as rclc supplies it at `rclc_executor_add_subscription`.

It keeps the `nros_` prefix DELIBERATELY, and that is the whole content of this row. rclc's same-named calls deliver a DESERIALISED message into caller-owned storage; these deliver CDR BYTES. Taking rclc's spelling for a byte-oriented entry point would be a name whose contract differs -- the `PollingSubscription::take()` failure, which had rclcpp's name, rclcpp's signature and the opposite contract, and cost a spinning loop with no compile error.

The faithful rclc-shaped entry point exists beside it and DOES take the name: `nros_executor_add_subscription_typed` (W5.a), reached per-message as `<Msg>_executor_add_subscription(exec, sub, &msg, cb, ctx, invocation)` -- rclc's six arguments in rclc's order. So the two shapes are distinguished by NAME rather than by a reader noticing which one deserialises, which is what RFC-0089 asks for.

c:executor_add_subscription_raw_with_inf.why: the raw + message-info form; see `c:publish_raw` and `rust:RawMessageInfo`.

c:executor_add_subscription_typed.why:
phase-417 W5.a — typed subscription delivery. rclc hands its callback a DESERIALISED message on a path with no allocator, by making the CALLER own the storage:

    rclc_executor_add_subscription(exec, sub, void *msg, callback, invocation)
    typedef void (*rclc_subscription_callback_t)(const void *);

Ours had no `msg` slot and delivered CDR bytes, so every ported rclc callback body had to be rewritten -- the largest porting cost this campaign measured. Many C rows justified the byte orientation with "no allocator"; rclc has no allocator on that path either, so the stated reason was refuted by the compared surface, which is worse than an unexplained divergence because it forecloses the fix.

ONE argument differs from rclc's, and it is forced: `nros_message_type_t` carries a type name, hash and max size but NO deserialiser slot, unlike rosidl's type support. So the function that writes this type into `msg` has to arrive from somewhere, and it sits immediately before `callback`, leaving every other argument in rclc's position. Codegen collapses it away -- `<Msg>_executor_add_subscription(exec, sub, &msg, cb, ctx, invocation)` is rclc's six in rclc's order -- so a ported line is unchanged.

A deserialise failure does NOT invoke the callback: dispatching would hand it `msg` still holding the PREVIOUS message dressed as the new one, which is exactly the compile-and-differ RFC-0089 forbids. The sample is dropped, `subscription_errors` increments, and a `#[cold]` reporter logs the sample length and return code through `nros_log` (never stdio -- issue 0589).

c:executor_get_publishers_info_by_topic.why: phase-381 W3/W4. Same verb as ROS 2; the RECEIVER differs. ROS 2 hangs the graph off a node because each Node/Context owns a participant; a nano-ros image opens ONE session for the whole image -- a session per node is RAM a 128 KiB target does not have -- and the Executor owns it. NOT a `rename`: the name follows the receiver, and the receiver is where the session is. The endpoint carries no QoS. The GRANTED profile is what answers 'why is nothing arriving', no backend can read one back yet, and reporting the remote's DECLARED profile would be a confident wrong answer -- so the field is absent here and the rmw ABI's `*_UNKNOWN` sentinels carry it at the vtable seam, which is that ABI's documented way to say 'could not determine'.

c:executor_wait_for_publishers.why:
phase-444. OUR spelling of upstream's `rcl_wait_for_publishers` — see `c:wait_for_publishers` for the decision, the RFC-0021 argument for why the one blocking member of the graph family is allowed to block, and why `Unsupported` returns at once instead of waiting out the budget.

c:get_zero_initialized_publisher.why: rcl's free-function spelling; ours is `nros_publisher_get_zero_initialized`, a method-style name on the type. See `c:get_zero_initialized_node`.

c:get_zero_initialized_subscription_cont.why: content-filtered topics are a DDS feature: the subscriber ships an SQL-ish expression the WRITER evaluates. Only one of our backends is DDS, and the filter would have to be a no-op on zenoh and XRCE -- a QoS-shaped promise two of three transports cannot keep. Same reasoning `rmw-api-parity.py` already records for `rmw_*_content_filter`.

c:message_type_t.why: the typesupport handle a publisher or subscription is created with. rosidl's `rosidl_message_type_support_t` carries function pointers into generated code plus an identifier used to pick a middleware-specific implementation at RUNTIME; ours names the one linked backend's descriptor, because an image has exactly one.

c:publish.why:
CORRECTED 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5), re-verdicted rename -> divergence. The previous text argued from `nros_publisher_publish`, a symbol that has never existed: the only occurrence of that spelling anywhere in the tree is a comment in `examples/native/c/custom-transport-loopback/src/main.c` recording that phase 212 replaced the never-defined name. Our C publish entry points are `nros_publish_raw(publisher, data, len)` for the byte form and the codegen'd per-message `<pkg>_<msg>_publish(publisher, msg)` for the typed form (`packs/c/message.h.jinja`, e.g. `std_msgs_msg_int32_publish`). BOTH already have rcl's shape -- a free function taking the publisher first -- so there is no free-function-vs-method rename here. The cited precedent does not apply either, twice over: `c:get_zero_initialized_publisher` is verdict DECLINED, i.e. it argues for KEEPING our spelling, and it declines because ours there IS method-style, which ours here is not.
What actually differs is the SHAPE, and a platform constraint is why. `rcl_publish(publisher, ros_message, allocation)` is ONE type-erased function over a `const void *` ROS message plus an `rmw_publisher_allocation_t *`. We have no runtime typesupport dispatch and no allocator, so the typed publish is generated per message type (concrete struct pointer, no typesupport lookup, serializes into a `NROS_PUB_BUFFER_SIZE` stack buffer) and the type-erased publish is byte-oriented. The generated typed helper lives in a message header, which the report drops as message plumbing -- that, not an absence, is why this row reads theirs-only.
The `_raw` suffix on the byte form is a separate and still-open question, tracked by the SERIALIZED -> RAW pair (`c:take_serialized_message`, `c:publish_serialized_message`). It is not this row's.

rename.resolution: Not a rename. The word and the free-function shape already match; the row's premise (nros_publisher_publish) was a symbol that does not exist. Re-verdicted to divergence, naming the two real differences and their constraints: no `rmw_publisher_allocation_t` (no allocator) and per-type codegen instead of a `const void *` (no runtime typesupport dispatch). No code change; no target name invented.

c:publish_raw.why: the ours-only half of the SERIALIZED -> RAW rename pair (`c:take_serialized_message`).

c:publish_serialized_message.why: ROS 2 says SERIALIZED for the pre-CDR byte form; ours is `nros_publish_raw`. This row became the SOLE owner of that decision on 2026-09-03: the receive half (`c:take_serialized_message`) landed with phase-379 W6 decision 1, which renamed `try_recv_raw` -> `take_serialized`, so publish is the only side still saying RAW. One word, used consistently on both sides, and ours is the one that has to move. (Symbol spelling corrected 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5): this row said `nros_cpp_publisher_publish_raw`; the C++ FFI symbol is `nros_cpp_publish_raw`.)

rename.resolution:
Target settled 2026-09-03 alongside the RECEIVE half, which did land: `nros_subscription_take_serialized` (`nros_generated.h:6459`) with `try_recv_raw` surviving as a `NROS_DEPRECATED_MSG` forwarder. This is the transmit half, unexecuted.

The `nros_`/`rcl_` prefix is NOT the difference — `normalize()` strips both symmetrically, so the keys reduce to `publish_raw` vs `publish_serialized_message`; `_message` and the module prefix stay dropped per `c:take_serialized_message`'s declined precedent.

Scope is wider than this C row implies: three ours-only halves are already rowed (`c:publish_raw`, `cpp:Publisher::publish_raw`, `rust:Publisher::publish_raw`), plus the `nros_cpp_publish_raw` FFI symbol and the C message template, which emits `return nros_publish_raw(...)` in generated code. Confirm the exact target symbol before executing — the row names the word `serialized` but never the symbol.

c:publisher_can_loan_messages.why:
asks whether the middleware supports loaning, so a caller can pick the zero-copy path at runtime. Ours is a compile-time property of the backend and nothing exposes it, so portable code cannot branch on it. Phase 379 W3.

VERDICT (phase-417 gap-verdict pass, 2026-09-21) — ABSENT, by the family verdict, not by a fresh argument. Upstream's TYPED loan is `absent`: no backend here delivers a struct in layout — uORB, the one that natively could, leaves `borrow_loaned_message` NULL (`packages/rmw/uorb/nros-rmw-uorb/src/vtable.cpp:90`) and takes bytes through `orb_publish`, and zenoh's slot (`nros-rmw-zenoh/src/lib.rs:439`, `zenoh_pub_loan`) is a token over a byte range. Our loan is zero-copy of the WIRE MESSAGE, which is an `extension`, not upstream's capability under a changed shape. That verdict is being recorded in RFC-0089 by the concurrent wave; this row applies it rather than re-deriving it.

SO THE PREDICATE IS `absent` FOR THE REASON RFC-0089 STATES ONCE: a member reached only through a refused family is absent, because the refusal already fired at the type. A ported program writes `if (pub->can_loan_messages()) { auto m = pub->borrow_loaned_message(); … }`; the branch it guards does not exist here, so answering the predicate under upstream's name promises the typed path and then fails at the next line. The BIT itself is real and already computed — `pub_state.can_loan_messages = vtable.borrow_loaned_message.is_some()` (`packages/rmw/cffi/src/lib.rs:2555`) — and may be surfaced under OUR byte-loan vocabulary whenever someone wants it. That would be a new `extension` row, not this one.

THE FAMILY VERDICT'S HOME is RFC-0089 Part V, "The loan family: two things called zero-copy" (`docs/design/0089-ros2-api-adoption-and-the-compile-or-conform-rule.md`) — cite it rather than re-deriving it here; the measurements above are this row's corroboration of it, not a second derivation.

VERDICT CORRECTED 2026-09-21, `gap` -> `declined`, and the reasoning above is
unchanged — it was already the reasoning for a decline. `gap` means "ROS 2 has
it, WE SHOULD TOO, and nobody has done it"; this row's own recorded verdict says
the opposite in as many words: the branch the predicate guards does not exist
here, answering it under upstream's name promises the typed path, and RFC-0089
Part V ("The loan family: two things called zero-copy") rules upstream's typed
loan `absent` because no backend we ship can deliver a struct in layout. A row
carrying `disposition: absent` under `verdict: gap` asserts both "we should
build this" and "the name does not exist", which cannot both be true, and it
was the `verdict` field that had not been moved when the disposition was
written.

NOT closed by building anything, deliberately. Issue 0814 records that the
lending path has never run on hardware, and `feature = "lending"` gates the byte
loan we DO have; implementing a predicate for a capability nobody has exercised
would answer `true` on a path with no evidence behind it. The BIT is still real
and still computed (`pub_state.can_loan_messages = vtable.borrow_loaned_message
.is_some()`), and surfacing it under OUR byte-loan vocabulary remains available
as a new `extension` row whenever someone wants it — which is a different row
from this one, as the paragraph above already says.

c:publisher_get_actual_qos.why:
reports the QoS an entity actually ended up with, which can differ from what its call site requested.

LANDED phase-444 (issue 1437) — `nros_publisher_get_actual_qos(const nros_publisher_t *, nros_qos_t *out)`. This row carries the argument for the whole family; the other five point here.

CONTRACT — the answer is upstream's, per policy: what the BACKEND GRANTED, and `NROS_QOS_*_UNKNOWN` for a policy it looked at and cannot determine. Not the request echoed back, which is what the seam did until issue 1437. The four `nros_qos_*_t` enums gained `UNKNOWN` and `SYSTEM_DEFAULT` in phase-444 so the profile can carry both answers; before that this accessor could not be written at all without inventing a concrete value, which is what this row said when it was a gap.

SHAPE — this is the one thing that stops `same`, and the reason is the platform. `rcl` returns `const rmw_qos_profile_t *`: an INTERIOR POINTER into the handle, which obliges every handle to RETAIN a profile. There is no allocator here, so "retain" means a field in a `#[repr(C)]` struct whose layout is this API's ABI — ~28 bytes of RAM per publisher, per subscription and per service endpoint, in EVERY image, including the ones that never call this. It also hands the caller a lifetime with no ownership type to enforce it (RFC-0018 / RFC-0022: the same reason no `create_*` returns an owning pointer). The status-plus-out-parameter shape is this API's own, and it buys one thing beyond the RAM: `rcl` encodes failure as NULL, which cannot distinguish "not initialized" from "registered but not yet added to an executor", and both are reachable states here.

HISTORY, kept because it is the reason the row exists. It was `declined` on the premise that QoS is selected at COMPILE time, so actual and requested are one value and an accessor would return its own input. That is false in both languages: QoS is a RUNTIME argument (`nros_publisher_init_with_options(..., const struct nros_qos_t *qos, ...)`) and a launch-lowered override table changes it AFTER the call site (`nros_node_set_qos_overrides`, folded in by `apply_qos_overrides`). Re-verdicted `gap` in phase-417; phase-428 W5 then measured that the SEAM's own answer was inverted — the out-struct arrived pre-loaded with the request and cyclonedds overwrote only the fields it could read, so a policy nobody looked at reported as granted. Issue 1437 fixed the seam and left the surface; this change is the surface.

c:publisher_get_context.why: reaches the context a publisher was created on. There is no separate context object -- see the init stage's `c:context_*`.

c:publisher_get_options.why: reads back the options a publisher was created with. `nros_publisher_options_t` ships (`nros_generated.h:2467-2474`) and `nros_publisher_init_with_options` takes it; what is missing is the READBACK -- nothing retains the struct on the handle and no `*_get_options` exists anywhere in our C surface, for any entity. CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417): this row said there is no runtime options struct. Seven ship and the correlator buckets all fourteen items `same` -- `nros_{node,publisher,subscription,service,client,action_client,action_server}_options_t` (`packages/api/nros-c/include/nros/nros_generated.h:1461,1729,2011,2474,2537,2556,2592`) plus a `*_get_default_options` for each, and `nros_node_options_t::domain_id_override` is a RUNTIME per-node domain. What is genuinely absent is the LIFECYCLE around one: no `*_options_copy`, no `*_options_fini`, and no `*_get_options` readback anywhere in the C surface.

c:publisher_get_rmw_handle.why: hands out the underlying rmw/rcl handle so a caller can bypass the API. Our RMW seam is the vtable in `nros/rmw_vtable.h` (RFC-0035) and is deliberately not reachable from an entity; see `c:node_get_rmw_handle`.

c:publisher_get_subscription_count.why:
how many subscriptions are matched, RIGHT NOW. We notify on change (`nros_event_publisher_count_cb_t` + `nros_count_status_t`) and never let a caller ask, so code that wants to skip work when nobody is listening has to keep its own mirror of the callback's last value. Both forms are useful and rclcpp ships both. Phase 379 W3.

VERDICT (phase-417 gap-verdict pass, 2026-09-21) — ADOPT-BOUNDED, and **THE REASON ABOVE IS FALSE.** It says "We notify on change (`nros_event_publisher_count_cb_t` + `nros_count_status_t`)". We do not. That callback carries `NROS_EVENT_LIVELINESS_LOST` and `NROS_EVENT_OFFERED_DEADLINE_MISSED` (`nros_generated.h:2018`), and its subscriber twin carries `REQUESTED_DEADLINE_MISSED` and `MESSAGE_LOST` (`:1967`). There is no `PUBLICATION_MATCHED` / `SUBSCRIPTION_MATCHED` event anywhere in the tree — grep `NROS_EVENT_` and count: five, none of them a match count. A caller keeping "its own mirror of the callback's last value" would be mirroring a different number.

WHAT DOES ANSWER IT is the graph counter phase-381 W4 shipped: `nros_executor_count_subscribers(topic)` / `count_publishers(topic)`, in all three languages, over slots Cyclone and zenoh both fill. ADOPT-BOUNDED rather than ADOPT because the two questions differ and the difference must be in the doc comment, not discovered: upstream counts the endpoints MATCHED to THIS entity (QoS-compatible peers of this publisher); the topic-wide count includes an endpoint whose QoS does not match, and on a backend with no QoS negotiation it cannot tell them apart. Weaker, non-inverting, and it answers the use case the row states — skip the work when nobody is listening.

VERDICT (phase-444, 2026-09-22) — DIVERGENCE. **SHIPPED, on upstream's name and a weakened signature**, which is what ADOPT-BOUNDED asked for:

  * C: `rcl_publisher_get_subscription_count(publisher, executor, out_count)` and `rcl_subscription_get_publisher_count(subscription, executor, out_count)` (`packages/api/nros-c/src/{publisher,subscription}.rs`, declared in `nros_generated.h`).
  * C++: `Publisher<M>::get_subscription_count(Executor&, size_t*) const` and `Subscription<M>::get_publisher_count(Executor&, size_t*) const`.
  * Rust: `EmbeddedPublisher::get_subscription_count(&Executor)` and `Subscription::get_publisher_count(&Executor)`.

TWO WEAKENINGS, both in the doc comment at every site rather than discovered. (1) THE QUESTION: upstream counts the endpoints MATCHED to THIS entity — peers whose QoS is compatible; we count every endpoint DISCOVERED on the topic, over the graph counter phase-381 W4 shipped. Non-inverting in the SAFE direction: a topic nobody joined still reads `0`, so "skip the work when nobody is listening" — the use this row states — is answered exactly, while an INCOMPATIBLE peer reads `1` where upstream reads `0` (you do work nobody receives, never the reverse). (2) THE RECEIVER: the executor is a parameter, because we open ONE transport session per image and the Executor owns it — the same receiver difference every graph verb carries. Both are what the compiler makes a porter notice, which is RFC-0089's mechanical-edit test.

AND `Unsupported` IS NOT `0`. A backend that cannot read the graph (XRCE) returns an error and does not write the out-parameter; collapsing that into a count would make a caller stop publishing on a backend that simply cannot tell. Pinned by `a_backend_with_no_graph_does_not_report_a_count_of_zero`.

The row stays a `divergence` and not a deletion because the SIGNATURE differs — the correlator files it `differs`, not `same`. On the Rust side the receiver differs too: the key `Publisher` is ours only as `nros_rmw::Publisher`, the RMW seam, and the user handle is `EmbeddedPublisher` (see `rust:Publisher::topic_name` for the same measurement).

c:publisher_get_zero_initialized.why: rcl's zero-init idiom under our naming; see `c:node_get_zero_initialized`.

c:publisher_impl_t.why: rcl's pimpl. Our handles carry their state inline because there is no allocator to put it behind a pointer; see the init stage's `c:context_*`.

c:publisher_init.why:
rcl's options-taking publisher constructor, and the one rcl name in this family we do not define. The CAPABILITY is present under our own spelling: `nros_publisher_init_with_options(pub, node, type_support, topic, const struct nros_publisher_options_t *)` (`nros_generated.h`), and rclc's default form ships under rclc's exact name as `rclc_publisher_init_default`. Ours says `_with_options` where rcl says bare `_init` because rcl has no second constructor to distinguish it from -- its `_init` IS the options-taking form -- while our surface spells the pair `_init_default` / `_init_with_options` across all five entities, so a reader who has seen one has seen them all. See `c:publisher_init_with_options` for the ours-only half and `c:publisher_get_options` for the readback rcl also has and we decline.

RE-VERDICTED 2026-09-13 (phase-417 W5.a follow-through), divergence -> extension. Both halves of the old reason were refuted, one by our own code and one by RFC-0089 itself, and they are recorded here rather than smoothed away.

It said: "the callback is bound to the ENTITY at creation (RFC-0041), so its type belongs to the subscription rather than to the executor's add call. rclc's counterpart is `rclc_subscription_callback_t`, passed to `rclc_executor_add_subscription` -- the `executor-owns-no-entity-storage` rule, seen as a type."

(2) THE RULE DOES NOT EXIST. `executor-owns-no-entity-storage` is cited by name in ten ledger rows and is defined nowhere in `docs/design/` (RFC-0089, "RFC-0041 does not decide this, and the rule cited instead does not exist"); RFC-0041's normative content is the DISPATCH MODEL, not a binding site. This row was prose citing prose.

WHAT THE DIFFERENCE ACTUALLY IS, now that the binding site and the invented rule are gone: the DATA contract, and it is the only thing left. Ours is `void (*)(const uint8_t *data, size_t len, void *context)` -- CDR bytes -- where rclc's `rclc_subscription_callback_t` is `void (*)(const void *msg)` over a DESERIALIZED message. NOTE WHAT DOES NOT APPEAR HERE ANY MORE: "no allocator". W5.a measured that reason and it was false -- rclc delivers a typed message with no allocator either, by making the caller own the storage, and so do we now. The byte callback survives because a caller that parses or FORWARDS its own payload (`packages/testing/nros-tests/bins/bridge-zenoh-to-*`) has no other shape, not because delivery costs a heap. The five C listener examples were ported off it in the same wave, so the byte path keeps only the callers that actually want bytes.

(1) THE QUESTION: upstream counts the endpoints MATCHED to THIS entity — peers whose QoS is compatible; we count every endpoint DISCOVERED on the topic, over the graph counter phase-381 W4 shipped. A backend that cannot read the graph (XRCE) returns an error and does not write the out-parameter; collapsing that into a count would make a caller stop publishing on a backend that simply cannot tell. phase-428 W5 (2026-09-06) ledgered a recorded sweep finding, RANKED-9, the whole class in one row: seven call sites across five verbs (`create_service` and `create_client` each appear twice).

UPSTREAM'S CONTRACT: `rclcpp::Node::create_*` either returns a usable entity or THROWS. A non-null return is a promise.

OURS NOW (`packages/api/nros-cpp/include/nros/nros.hpp`, the `rclcpp::Node` adapter), re-measured 2026-09-23: every factory passes the inner `nros::Result` to `detail::require_created` (`:328`) — `create_publisher` at `:519`, `create_subscription` `:584`, `create_wall_timer` `:637`, `create_service` `:686` / `:702`, `create_client` `:727` / `:743` — which on failure calls `abort_failed_create` (`:320`): `NROS_ERROR` naming the verb, the entity name and the `nros::ErrorCode`, then the `NROS_RCLCPP_ABORT_FAILED_CREATE` text (`log.hpp:203`) naming the underlying `nros::Node` verbs that return the `Result` for a caller who wants to handle it, then `std::abort()`. `require_created` takes the `Result` BY VALUE so the `[[nodiscard]]` is consumed there and cannot be dropped a second time. A returned pointer is therefore an initialised entity, which is upstream's promise minus the throw.

HOW A USER FINDS OUT: the process dies at the failing create naming it. The remaining silence is one frame UP — constructing a `Node` before `rclcpp::init()` yields `initialized() == false` with no diagnostic until the first create (`cpp:Node::Node`), and `rclcpp::spin` / `spin_some` (`:894` / `:901`) still return without a word on such a node; with every create aborting, that path is only reachable by a node that created nothing.

WHY `divergence` AND NOT `gap`. The difference is "upstream throws, we terminate", and no exceptions is one of the constraints SCHEMA.md names as sanctioning a divergence. RFC-0018 states it twice — "No exceptions: compile with `-fno-exceptions`" and the Key Differences row "Exceptions for errors -> `Result` return values / No exceptions on embedded" — and `nros.hpp:290-320` weighs each alternative (a `Result`-returning overload, a null `shared_ptr`, an `ok()` flag) and concludes that aborting at the create is the loudest answer available. Same name and same arity as `rclcpp::create_publisher`, and the RETURN TYPE differs: ours is `ResultOf<Publisher<M>>`, upstream's is `std::shared_ptr<Publisher<MessageT>>`. Both halves of that are forced. We do not return a `shared_ptr` because a freestanding target has none (RFC-0018, RFC-0096), and we do not signal failure by throwing because the API does not throw -- so the value has to carry the error, which is what `ResultOf` is. A ported file that discards the result compiles either way and silently loses the failure report, which is exactly why a return-only difference is `same:ret` and needs a disposition rather than passing as a match.

The row is AUTHORED HERE rather than earlier because until phase-442 W2 the name carried TWO overloads -- this one and the now-DELETED `std_compat.hpp`'s `Result create_publisher(Node&, Publisher<M>&, const std::string&, QoS)` -- whose differing arities put the key outside the `same` bucket and so outside `--require-disposition`'s reach. Deleting the dead std vocabulary did not create the divergence; it stopped masking it. Two rows already pointed here -- `cpp:create_subscription` and `cpp:create_publisher_factory` both say 'see `cpp:create_publisher`' -- against a key that did not exist.

The always-available spelling with no return-shape question is the method `Node::create_publisher(out, topic, qos)` (`cpp:Node::create_publisher`), which is what the factory wraps.

phase-456 W1 — the capturing sibling of `rust:Executor::add_arena_subscription_c_callback`, and ours-only for the same reason that row gives: this is the IMPERATIVE Rust API carrying the storage strategy in the name. What the suffix adds is a LIFETIME, not a dispatch: the plain form passes the caller's `context` through untouched, so the caller must keep it alive and unmoved for as long as the executor runs, while this one COPIES the caller's capture into the arena entry and repoints `context` at the entry's own copy. Nothing of the caller's is referenced after the call returns.

rclrs has no counterpart and cannot: its subscription owns a boxed closure behind an `Arc`, so the question of where a capture lives does not arise. Ours arises because the C++ API on top has no allocator, and it is what lets a C++ entity become a handle instead of an object the arena knows by address (RFC-0096 D9 revision 3).

A capture longer than `CALLBACK_CAPTURE_BYTES` (`4 * size_of::<*const ()>()`, the same expression as the C++ `NROS_CPP_CALLBACK_CAPACITY`) is REJECTED rather than truncated, because the C++ side asserts the same bound at compile time and reaching the runtime check means the two constants have drifted.

rust:Executor::subscription_handle.why:
issue 1437 / phase-444 — resolves an arena entry index to the transport handle it begins with, so the C and C++ `*_get_actual_qos` accessors answer on the CALLBACK road as well as the poll one. A callback-registered entity is owned by the executor arena and the user's handle is bookkeeping: its inline storage is untouched and the only identity it carries is the index. An accessor reading that storage would serve the poll road and return an absence on the road a ported `rclcpp` node actually takes.

rclrs has no counterpart because it has no arena: entities are `Arc`s the user holds (RFC-0022 / the `no-arc-self` rule), so there is nothing to resolve an index against. That is the platform difference, not a naming one — the arena exists to avoid `alloc`.

One layer below the user API, alongside `rust:Executor::action_client_core_mut` and `rust:Executor::service_client_entry_mut`, which are the same shape and carry the same complaint (issue 0784: `pub` from `nros::` beside the user API). It differs from those two in reading ONLY the handle, which is why one function serves every entry SHAPE of its kind rather than naming one monomorphisation — every arena entry is `#[repr(C)]` with its handle first, pinned by `arena::handle_offset_tests`.

Twelve subscription entry shapes; all twelve begin with `RmwSubscriber`.

cpp:PollSubscription.why:
phase-456 W2b — the poll-style subscription, split out of `Subscription<M>`. Ours-only because of its OWNERSHIP, not its method names: a caller declares it in its own frame, it holds the `RmwSubscriber` in `storage_`, nothing dispatches, and the caller drains it with `take()`. Upstream has no such entity — every `rclcpp::Subscription` is owned by the node and driven by an executor, and upstream's poll shape is a `WaitSet` reporting an executor-owned entity ready, not a subscriber the caller stores.

WHY IT WAS SPLIT, measured. One class served both owners behind a `callback_mode_` flag, and `storage_` is filled only on the poll path — the arena owns the subscriber on the other one. So a `take()` on a callback-mode object passed 656 value-initialized zero bytes to `nros_cpp_subscription_take_serialized`, which does `&mut *(storage as *mut RmwSubscriber)` (`packages/api/nros-cpp/src/subscription.rs`). `initialized_` was true, so nothing refused. `nros.hpp` described that call as answering `NotInitialized`; it did not.

cpp:PollSubscription::PollSubscription<M.why: the constructor set of an ours-only type: a default constructor plus move operations, with copies deleted. See `cpp:PollSubscription`. Unlike `cpp:Subscription::Subscription<M>` the MOVE is sound here and phase-456 W2b is why: this half owns its subscriber and relocates it through `nros_cpp_subscription_relocate`, and no arena entry holds its address. The hazard that row records belongs to the dispatch half, which is where it stayed.

cpp:PollSubscription::get_topic_name.why: the topic this subscriber was created for, kept C++-side since phase 87.6 (the runtime handle does not store it). Upstream's `SubscriptionBase::get_topic_name` is the same accessor on the entity `cpp:Subscription::get_topic_name` corresponds to; this is the ours-only poll type's copy of it.

cpp:PollSubscription::take.why: phase-456 W2b — the same operation `cpp:Subscription::take` records, on the class that can perform it. Read that row for the trade; the short form is that upstream's `take` is called on an executor-owned entity after a `WaitSet` reports it ready, and we have no wait set, so the caller-owned subscriber is the thing that can answer. The second parameter still differs: rclcpp's is `take(ROSMessageType&, MessageInfo&)` and ours takes the message only, because most backends carry no per-sample message info and the one that does exposes it as `take_serialized_with_attachment`.

cpp:PollSubscription::take_serialized.why: phase-456 W2b — see `cpp:Subscription::take_serialized` for the trade and `cpp:PollSubscription::take` for the same one on the typed form. Upstream's is `SubscriptionBase::take_serialized(SerializedMessage&, MessageInfo&)`; ours writes into a caller-supplied `(uint8_t*, size_t, size_t&)` because there is no allocator to grow a `SerializedMessage` with.

cpp:Subscription::take_serialized.why:
phase-456 W2b — this row is NEW because the split made the name theirs-only. `SubscriptionBase::take_serialized(SerializedMessage&, MessageInfo&)` is upstream's, and it is reached on an entity the node owns, after a `WaitSet` reports it ready. Ours is `nros::PollSubscription<M>::take_serialized`, on the entity the CALLER owns, because we have no wait set and the dispatch entity has no receive buffer to take from — the arena does.

Stated plainly because it is a cost: until W2b the name sat on `Subscription<M>` and correlated, so no row was needed. It correlated on a class where half the objects could not perform it, which is the defect W2b removed; the parity report is now accurate about a difference that already existed.
